::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- turn texts into **sequences of word ids** and **pad** them to a fixed length;
- explain what an **embedding** layer learns;
- describe the **update** and **reset** gates of a GRU and compare a GRU with an LSTM (gates, memory, number of parameters);
- fit GRU and LSTM classifiers with `layer_gru()` / `layer_lstm()` and early stopping;
- compare them honestly with a **penalised bag-of-words logistic regression**, and choose a classification threshold.
:::

## Running this lesson

The model chunks need **keras3** and a backend (see [lesson 61](61-dl-setup.qmd)); the IMDB reviews are downloaded by keras the first time (about 20 MB). The baseline uses the CRAN packages **glmnet** and **Matrix**. The results on this page were computed once and frozen. Without keras, the keras code is shown but not run, and numbers that depend on it read "*not computed*". The small base-R examples (padding, gates, parameter counts) run everywhere.
:::

## 1. Why read text in order?

A film website receives thousands of reviews a day and wants to know which are positive and which are negative. Each review is a piece of text of variable length; the label is 1 (positive) or 0 (negative). This is binary classification, as in [lesson 41](../09-regression/41-logistic-regression.qmd) — but the "predictors" are words.

The simplest approach ignores word order: count which words appear (a **bag of words**) and fit a logistic regression. It works surprisingly well. But order sometimes matters: "not good, not bad, actually great" and "great? actually not good" contain almost the same words. A **recurrent network** reads the words one at a time, like the LSTM read hours of electricity demand in [lesson 64](64-lstm.qmd). In this lesson we use the **Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)**, a simpler relative of the LSTM, and we check whether reading in order actually pays off.

## 2. The data: 50,000 movie reviews

The IMDB dataset (Maas et al., 2011) ships with keras: 25,000 training and 25,000 test reviews, half positive and half negative. The reviews are already **tokenised**: each word has been replaced by an integer id, with frequent words getting small ids. We keep only the 10,000 most frequent words; rarer words become a special "unknown" id.

```{r}
#| label: import
#| eval: !expr has_keras
max_words <- 10000
imdb <- dataset_imdb(num_words = max_words)
x_train_raw <- imdb$train$x          # a list: one integer vector per review
y_train     <- imdb$train$y          # 0 = negative, 1 = positive
x_test_raw  <- imdb$test$x
y_test      <- imdb$test$y
c(train = length(x_train_raw), test = length(x_test_raw))
table(y_train)
```

```{r}
#| label: first-review
#| eval: !expr has_keras
head(x_train_raw[[1]], 12)
```

To read a review we need the dictionary. Ids 0, 1 and 2 are reserved (padding, "start of review", "unknown word"), so the word with dictionary index $k$ has id $k + 3$:

```{r}
#| label: decode
#| eval: !expr has_keras
word_index <- dataset_imdb_word_index()            # word -> dictionary index
index_word <- setNames(names(word_index), unlist(word_index) + 3)
decode <- function(ids) {
  words <- index_word[as.character(ids)]
  words[ids == 1] <- "<start>"
  words[ids == 2] <- "<unk>"
  paste(words, collapse = " ")
}
substr(decode(x_train_raw[[1]]), 1, 300)
```

Reviews have very different lengths:

```{r}
#| label: lengths
#| eval: !expr has_keras
len <- lengths(x_train_raw)
summary(len)
mean(len > 200)
```

The median review has `r show_num(median(len), 0)` words, but `r show_num(round(100 * mean(len > 200)), 0)`% are longer than 200 words.

## 3. From texts to a matrix: padding

A network trains on **mini-batches**, so all sequences in a batch must have the same length $T$. We **pad** short reviews with the id 0 and **truncate** long ones. By default keras pads and truncates at the *start* ("pre"): it keeps the last $T$ words and puts the zeros in front. Here is the same logic in base R on three toy "reviews":

```{r}
#| label: pad-toy
pad_pre <- function(seqs, maxlen) {
  t(vapply(seqs, \(s) {
    s <- tail(s, maxlen)                       # keep the last maxlen ids
    c(rep(0L, maxlen - length(s)), s)          # zeros in front
  }, integer(maxlen)))
}
toy <- list(c(5L, 12L, 7L), c(3L, 9L, 4L, 8L, 2L, 6L), 11L)
pad_pre(toy, maxlen = 4)
```

The second toy review lost its first two ids; the others got leading zeros. Pre-padding suits recurrent networks: the network's final state, which is used for the prediction, is reached right after the *real* words rather than after a long run of zeros.

```{r}
#| label: pad
#| eval: !expr has_keras
max_len <- 200
x_train_pad <- pad_sequences(x_train_raw, maxlen = max_len)
x_test_pad  <- pad_sequences(x_test_raw,  maxlen = max_len)
dim(x_train_pad)
```

We set aside 15% of the training reviews as a **validation set** (for early stopping and for tuning the baseline). The test set is used once, at the end.

```{r}
#| label: split
#| eval: !expr has_keras
set.seed(123)
va_idx <- sample(nrow(x_train_pad), size = round(0.15 * nrow(x_train_pad)))
X_tr <- x_train_pad[-va_idx, ];  y_tr <- y_train[-va_idx]
X_va <- x_train_pad[va_idx, ];   y_va <- y_train[va_idx]
c(train = nrow(X_tr), valid = nrow(X_va))
```

## 4. The baseline: a penalised bag-of-words model

Before any network, a model that ignores order. Each review becomes a row of 10,000 columns, one per word, containing $\log(1 + \text{count})$. Most entries are zero, so we store the matrix in **sparse** form (only the non-zero values). A lasso logistic regression ([lesson 43](../09-regression/43-penalized-regression.qmd)) then picks the useful words; we choose the penalty $\lambda$ with the **same validation set** the networks will use.

```{r}
#| label: bow-fun
#| eval: !expr has_keras
bow_matrix <- function(seqs, V = max_words) {
  m <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = rep(seq_along(seqs), lengths(seqs)),
                            j = unlist(seqs), x = 1,
                            dims = c(length(seqs), V))   # repeated words summed
  m@x <- log1p(m@x)                                      # dampen counts
  m
}
bow_all  <- bow_matrix(x_train_raw)
bow_tr   <- bow_all[-va_idx, ]
bow_va   <- bow_all[va_idx, ]
bow_test <- bow_matrix(x_test_raw)
```

We also need a way to score probabilities. The **AUC** is the probability that a randomly chosen positive review gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one; it can be computed from ranks (it is the Mann–Whitney statistic of [lesson 36](../08-inference/36-nonparametric-tests.qmd), rescaled):

```{r}
#| label: auc-fun
auc_rank <- function(p, y) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
scores <- function(p, y) c(accuracy = mean((p >= 0.5) == y), auc = auc_rank(p, y))
```

```{r}
#| label: bow-fit
#| eval: !expr has_keras
bow_fit <- glmnet::glmnet(bow_tr, y_tr, family = "binomial")    # lasso path
p_va_path <- predict(bow_fit, bow_va, type = "response")       # one column per lambda
val_auc_path <- apply(p_va_path, 2, auc_rank, y = y_va)
best_lambda <- bow_fit$lambda[which.max(val_auc_path)]
p_va_bow <- as.vector(predict(bow_fit, bow_va, s = best_lambda, type = "response"))
scores(p_va_bow, y_va)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

`glmnet()` fits the lasso for a whole sequence of penalties; we keep the one with the highest validation AUC. Accuracy is the share of validation reviews classified correctly at the threshold 0.5, AUC the ranking quality. A validation AUC of `r show_num(scores(p_va_bow, y_va)[["auc"]])` from a model that does not know word order is the bar the recurrent networks have to clear. Note that the bag of words sees the *whole* review, while the networks will see only its last 200 words.
:::

A bonus of the linear model: its coefficients are readable.

```{r}
#| label: bow-words
#| eval: !expr has_keras
b <- as.vector(coef(bow_fit, s = best_lambda))[-1]     # drop the intercept
top <- function(idx) unname(index_word[as.character(idx)])
list(positive = top(order(b, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]),
     negative = top(order(b)[1:10]))
```

## 5. Embeddings: words as vectors

A network could receive each word as a "one-hot" vector of 10,000 zeros and a single one, but that is wasteful and says nothing about which words are similar. An **embedding layer** is a look-up table: a matrix $E$ with one row of $d$ numbers for each word id. Word $w_t$ is replaced by the row $e_t = E[w_t, ]$. The entries of $E$ are ordinary weights, learned by backpropagation together with the rest of the network, so words that play a similar role for the task ("excellent", "superb") tend to end up with similar vectors. With 10,000 words and $d = 32$, the embedding has $10{,}000 \times 32 =$ `r format(10000 * 32, big.mark = ",")` parameters — by far the largest part of our models.

## 6. The GRU: two gates instead of three

Lesson 64 explained why a plain RNN forgets: the gradient is multiplied at every step by a factor that is usually smaller than 1. The LSTM fixed this with a separate **cell state** and three gates. The **Gated Recurrent Unit** (Cho et al., 2014) keeps the idea but simplifies it: there is only the hidden state $h_t$, and two gates.

| Gate | Question it answers | LSTM counterpart |
|---|---|---|
| **Update** gate $z_t$ | How much of the old state should I keep, and how much should I replace with new content? | Forget and input gates together |
| **Reset** gate $r_t$ | When proposing new content, how much of the old state should I look at? | (no direct counterpart) |

The update gate is the key idea. The new state is a **weighted average** of the old state and a candidate $\tilde h_t$ built from the current word:

$$
h_t = z_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) \odot \tilde h_t .
$$

When $z_t$ is close to 1 the state is copied forward almost unchanged; when it is close to 0 it is overwritten. Because the gate depends on the input, the network can learn to *keep* its memory through unimportant words and *write* only when something informative arrives.

Let us watch this in base R with a single unit and hand-chosen weights. The input is a "+1" event at step 1, nothing for 14 steps, a "−1" event at step 16, then nothing again. The plain RNN uses $h_t = \tanh(2x_t + 0.5\,h_{t-1})$. The gated unit uses $z_t = \sigma(4 - 8|x_t|)$, which is about 0.98 when nothing happens and about 0.02 when an event arrives.

```{r}
#| label: gate-demo
x_seq <- c(1, rep(0, 14), -1, rep(0, 14))
plain_rnn <- function(x) {
  h <- numeric(length(x)); prev <- 0
  for (t in seq_along(x)) { prev <- tanh(2 * x[t] + 0.5 * prev); h[t] <- prev }
  h
}
gated_unit <- function(x) {
  h <- numeric(length(x)); prev <- 0
  for (t in seq_along(x)) {
    z <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(4 - 8 * abs(x[t]))))     # update gate
    prev <- z * prev + (1 - z) * tanh(2 * x[t])   # keep or overwrite
    h[t] <- prev
  }
  h
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gate
#| fig-cap: "Hidden state of a plain recurrent unit and of a gated (GRU-like) unit after an input event at steps 1 and 16. The plain unit forgets within a few steps; the gated unit keeps the information until a new event overwrites it."
gate_df <- data.frame(step = seq_along(x_seq),
                      plain = plain_rnn(x_seq), gated = gated_unit(x_seq)) |>
  pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "unit", values_to = "state")
ggplot(gate_df, aes(step, state, colour = unit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "time step", y = "hidden state h", colour = NULL)
```

After 14 quiet steps the plain unit's state is `r signif(plain_rnn(x_seq)[15], 2)` — the first event is forgotten — while the gated unit still holds `r round(gated_unit(x_seq)[15], 2)`. In a real GRU nobody chooses these weights: the gates are small sigmoid layers whose weights are learned from data.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the GRU equations and its parameter count

With input $x_t \in \mathbb R^p$ and $u$ units (this is the convention used by Keras and by Cho et al.; some books swap the roles of $z_t$ and $1 - z_t$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \sigma(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z) && \text{update gate}\\
r_t &= \sigma(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r) && \text{reset gate}\\
\tilde h_t &= \tanh\big(W_h x_t + r_t \odot (U_h h_{t-1}) + b_h\big) && \text{candidate}\\
h_t &= z_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t) \odot \tilde h_t .
\end{aligned}
$$

There are **three** blocks of weights (LSTM: four). Keras applies the reset gate after the recurrent multiplication, as written above (`reset_after = TRUE`), which needs a second bias vector per block, so a GRU layer has $3\,(u(u+p) + 2u)$ parameters, against $4\,(u(u+p) + u)$ for an LSTM. Along the direct path, $\partial h_t / \partial h_{t-1} = z_t$ (element-wise): when the update gate stays near 1, the gradient passes back through many steps — the same trick as the LSTM's forget gate.
:::

```{r}
#| label: param-count
gru_params  <- function(u, p) 3 * (u * (u + p) + 2 * u)
lstm_params <- function(u, p) 4 * (u * (u + p) + u)
c(gru = gru_params(32, 32), lstm = lstm_params(32, 32))
```

With 32 units reading 32-dimensional embeddings, the GRU layer has about a quarter fewer parameters than the LSTM layer. GRU versus LSTM in one table:

| | LSTM ([lesson 64](64-lstm.qmd)) | GRU |
|---|---|---|
| States carried along the sequence | hidden state $h_t$ and cell state $c_t$ | hidden state $h_t$ only |
| Gates | forget, input, output | update, reset |
| Weight blocks | 4 | 3 |
| Typical behaviour | slightly more flexible; sometimes better on long, complex sequences | faster per epoch; often similar accuracy |

Neither is better in general. In published comparisons they usually perform similarly, and the difference depends on the task; the practical advice is to try both with the same protocol.

## 7. Building the networks

Both models have the same structure: embedding (32 dimensions) → one recurrent layer of 32 units → a sigmoid output. The `dropout` argument of the recurrent layer randomly drops parts of its input at each step during training. A small function avoids writing the model twice:

```{r}
#| label: build-fun
#| eval: !expr has_keras
build_text_model <- function(type = c("gru", "lstm"), units = 32) {
  rnn_layer <- switch(match.arg(type), gru = layer_gru, lstm = layer_lstm)
  model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = max_len) |>
    layer_embedding(input_dim = max_words, output_dim = 32) |>
    rnn_layer(units = units, dropout = 0.2) |>
    layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
  model |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-3),
                   loss = "binary_crossentropy",
                   metrics = list("accuracy", metric_auc(name = "auc")))
  model
}
set_random_seed(123)
gru <- build_text_model("gru")
gru
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- The embedding layer turns each review, a vector of 200 ids, into a $200 \times 32$ matrix: Output Shape `(None, 200, 32)`. Its `r format(10000 * 32, big.mark = ",")` parameters are the word vectors.
- The GRU reads the 200 steps and returns only its **final** hidden state, `(None, 32)`, with `r gru_params(32, 32)` parameters (Section 6).
- The dense layer maps those 32 numbers to $P(\text{positive})$: $32 + 1 = 33$ parameters.
:::

## 8. Training with early stopping

As in lessons 62 and 64, early stopping watches the validation loss and restores the best weights. We also record the training time, since speed is one of the arguments for a GRU.

```{r}
#| label: train-fun
#| eval: !expr has_keras
train_text_model <- function(model, epochs = 15) {
  early_stop <- callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 2,
                                        restore_best_weights = TRUE)
  seconds <- system.time(
    history <- model |> fit(
      x = X_tr, y = y_tr,
      validation_data = list(X_va, y_va),
      epochs = epochs, batch_size = 128,
      callbacks = list(early_stop), verbose = 0
    )
  )[["elapsed"]]
  list(history = history, seconds = seconds)
}
gru_run <- train_text_model(gru)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-history-gru
#| fig-cap: "Learning curves of the GRU: loss and AUC on training and validation reviews."
#| eval: !expr has_keras
as.data.frame(gru_run$history) |>
  filter(!is.na(value), metric %in% c("loss", "auc")) |>
  ggplot(aes(epoch, value, colour = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Epoch", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

Text models overfit quickly: the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss typically reaches its minimum after only a few epochs. Training stopped after `r show_num(length(gru_run$history$metrics$loss), 0)` epochs (`r show_num(gru_run$seconds, 0)` seconds on the instructor's laptop CPU).

Now the LSTM, with the same seed, data, settings and early stopping:

```{r}
#| label: train-lstm
#| eval: !expr has_keras
set_random_seed(123)
lstm <- build_text_model("lstm")
lstm_run <- train_text_model(lstm)
```

## 9. The comparison on the test set

Only now do we use the 25,000 test reviews.

```{r}
#| label: test-compare
#| eval: !expr has_keras
p_test <- list(
  bag_of_words = as.vector(predict(bow_fit, bow_test, s = best_lambda,
                                   type = "response")),
  gru  = as.vector(predict(gru,  x_test_pad, verbose = 0)),
  lstm = as.vector(predict(lstm, x_test_pad, verbose = 0))
)
results <- tibble::tibble(
  model   = names(p_test),
  params  = c(sum(b != 0), gru$count_params(), lstm$count_params()),
  seconds = c(NA, gru_run$seconds, lstm_run$seconds),
  accuracy = sapply(p_test, \(p) scores(p, y_test)[["accuracy"]]),
  auc      = sapply(p_test, auc_rank, y = y_test)
)
results
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `params` is the number of non-zero word coefficients for the lasso and the number of weights for the networks. `seconds` is the training time (the lasso path is not timed; it takes well under a minute).
- Test AUC: bag of words `r show_num(results$auc[1])`, GRU `r show_num(results$auc[2])`, LSTM `r show_num(results$auc[3])`. With 25,000 test reviews, differences in the second decimal are real; differences in the third decimal are within run-to-run variation (lesson 61, Section 8).
- The usual finding on these data is that GRU and LSTM perform very similarly, and that the bag-of-words lasso is **close** to both. Reading in order helps with phrases like "not good", but much of the sentiment is carried by individual words. The network also sees only the last 200 words of each review.
:::

## 10. From probabilities to decisions

A probability becomes a label only when we choose a threshold. At 0.5, the GRU's confusion matrix and the usual summaries are:

```{r}
#| label: confusion
#| eval: !expr has_keras
pred <- as.integer(p_test$gru >= 0.5)
cm <- table(truth = factor(y_test, levels = 0:1), pred = factor(pred, levels = 0:1))
cm
tp <- cm["1", "1"]; tn <- cm["0", "0"]; fp <- cm["0", "1"]; fn <- cm["1", "0"]
precision <- tp / (tp + fp)
recall    <- tp / (tp + fn)
c(accuracy = (tp + tn) / sum(cm), precision = precision, recall = recall,
  f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall))
```

**Precision** answers "of the reviews flagged positive, how many are?"; **recall** "of the positive reviews, how many did we flag?"; **F1** is their harmonic mean. If a marketing team wants to quote only reviews that are surely positive, raise the threshold (higher precision, lower recall); choose it on the **validation** set, never on the test set.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Skipping the bag-of-words baseline.** A penalised linear model on word counts is fast, interpretable and often nearly as good as a recurrent network.
2. **Forgetting what padding and truncation do.** With `maxlen = 200` the model never sees the beginning of long reviews; with post-padding, an RNN's final state is reached after a long run of zeros.
3. **Choosing the penalty, the threshold or the number of epochs on the test set.** All tuning uses the validation set.
4. **Expecting the GRU to beat the LSTM (or vice versa).** They usually perform similarly; compare them with the same data, seed and early stopping.
5. **Using `set.seed()` to make keras reproducible.** Use `set_random_seed()`; `set.seed()` only controls R's own random numbers (here, the validation split).
6. **Ignoring the reserved ids.** 0 = padding, 1 = start, 2 = unknown word; the vocabulary size passed to `layer_embedding()` must be at least the largest id + 1.
:::

## 11. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What does an update gate value close to 1 mean in a GRU?

Keep the previous hidden state almost unchanged and ignore the new candidate: the unit "remembers" through this step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. How many parameters does `layer_gru(units = 16)` have when it reads 8-dimensional embeddings? And an LSTM of the same size?

GRU: $3\,(16 \cdot (16 + 8) + 2 \cdot 16) = 3 \cdot 416 = 1248$. LSTM: $4\,(16 \cdot 24 + 16) = 4 \cdot 400 = 1600$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A review has 350 words and `maxlen = 200` with the default settings. Which words does the network see?

The last 200: `pad_sequences()` truncates at the start (`truncating = "pre"`) by default.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Why is an embedding layer better than one-hot inputs?

It replaces 10,000-dimensional sparse vectors by short dense vectors that are learned for the task, so words with a similar role can get similar representations, and the following layers need far fewer weights.
:::

## 12. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — predict the output.** Without running it, write down `pad_pre(list(c(4L, 8L), c(1L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 7L)), maxlen = 3)`. What would keras return with `padding = "post"` and `truncating = "post"`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Default ("pre"): rows `0 4 8` and `3 5 7`. With `padding = "post", truncating = "post"`: rows `4 8 0` and `1 2 3` — zeros at the end, and the *first* three ids kept.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — count the parameters.** The original version of this lesson used a 128-dimensional embedding followed by `layer_bidirectional(layer_gru(units = 64))`, which runs one GRU left-to-right and one right-to-left and concatenates their final states. How many parameters does the bidirectional layer have, and what is its output size?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
One GRU: $3\,(64 \cdot (64 + 128) + 2 \cdot 64) = 3 \cdot 12{,}416 = 37{,}248$. Two directions: $74{,}496$. The output concatenates two 64-vectors: shape `(None, 128)`. You can check with `gru_params(64, 128) * 2`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — a bidirectional GRU.** Fit the original lesson's architecture (embedding 128, bidirectional GRU 64, dense 64 ReLU, dropout 0.3, sigmoid output) with the same split and early stopping, and add it to `results`. Is the extra size worth it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set_random_seed(123)
bigru <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = max_len) |>
  layer_embedding(input_dim = max_words, output_dim = 128) |>
  layer_bidirectional(layer_gru(units = 64, dropout = 0.2)) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
bigru |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3), loss = "binary_crossentropy",
                 metrics = list(metric_auc(name = "auc")))
bigru_run <- train_text_model(bigru)
p_bigru <- as.vector(predict(bigru, x_test_pad, verbose = 0))
scores(p_bigru, y_test)
```
The model has about 1.36 million parameters (mostly the embedding) and takes several times longer per epoch. Its test AUC is typically within about a hundredth of the small GRU: on this task the extra capacity buys little.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — GRU for electricity demand.** In [lesson 64](64-lstm.qmd), replace `layer_lstm(units = 32)` with `layer_gru(units = 32)` and keep everything else (windows, split, callbacks). Compare test RMSE, number of parameters and training time with the LSTM and with the AR(48) baseline.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set_random_seed(123)
gru_ts <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(L, 1)) |>
  layer_gru(units = 32) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1)
gru_ts |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3), loss = "mse")
secs <- system.time(
  gru_ts |> fit(w_train$X, w_train$y,
                validation_data = list(w_valid$X, w_valid$y),
                epochs = 30, batch_size = 128, callbacks = callbacks, verbose = 0)
)[["elapsed"]]
forecasts$gru <- to_mwh(as.vector(predict(gru_ts, w_test$X, verbose = 0)))
score(forecasts)
c(params = gru_ts$count_params(), seconds = secs)
```
The GRU layer has $3\,(32 \cdot 33 + 64) = 3360$ parameters against 4352 for the LSTM. Its test RMSE is usually very close to the LSTM's, and both should be compared with AR(48), which uses the same inputs.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — interpret the errors.** Find the 5 test reviews where the GRU is most confidently wrong (largest $|y - \hat p|$) and read them with `decode()`. What do they have in common?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
wrong <- order(abs(y_test - p_test$gru), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
data.frame(truth = y_test[wrong], p_gru = round(p_test$gru[wrong], 3))
for (i in wrong) cat(substr(decode(x_test_raw[[i]]), 1, 400), "\n\n")
```
Typical cases: sarcasm, reviews that describe a bad plot before praising the film (or the reverse), long reviews whose opinion is in the part cut off by truncation, and labels that seem debatable. Errors like these are a reminder that the model learns word patterns, not opinions.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 6 — is reading in order worth it?** Compute a 95% paired bootstrap interval for the difference in test AUC between the GRU and the bag-of-words lasso (resample the same test reviews for both, 500 replicates). Then write two sentences for a non-technical manager recommending one model.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set.seed(1)
d <- replicate(500, {
  i <- sample(length(y_test), replace = TRUE)
  auc_rank(p_test$gru[i], y_test[i]) - auc_rank(p_test$bag_of_words[i], y_test[i])
})
quantile(d, c(0.025, 0.975))
```
With 25,000 test reviews the interval is narrow, so even a small difference can be "significant". The recommendation should weigh its size against cost: if the GRU gains only about a hundredth of AUC, the lasso — which trains in seconds, runs anywhere and shows which words drive the prediction — is a defensible choice.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dataset_imdb(num_words = )` | Tokenised movie reviews (integer ids) |
| `pad_sequences(x, maxlen = )` | Pad / truncate to a fixed length (default: at the start) |
| `layer_embedding(input_dim, output_dim)` | Learned look-up table of word vectors |
| Update gate $z_t$, reset gate $r_t$ | Keep-or-overwrite, and how much past to use for the candidate |
| `layer_gru(units = , dropout = )` | GRU layer; $3(u(u+p) + 2u)$ parameters |
| `layer_lstm()`, `layer_bidirectional()` | LSTM; read the sequence in both directions |
| `glmnet::glmnet()` on a sparse bag of words | The baseline to beat |
| Precision, recall, F1, threshold | Turning probabilities into decisions |

- A GRU is a simplified LSTM: one state, two gates, three weight blocks; in practice the two perform similarly.
- Texts become padded sequences of ids, then dense vectors through an embedding.
- A penalised bag-of-words model is fast, interpretable and often close to the recurrent networks; always report it.
- All tuning (penalty, epochs, threshold) uses the validation set; the test set is used once.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
